title: Act III, Scene V
focus: parting at dawn and Capulet's rage

teacherSummary.text: At dawn the lovers argue whether it is the nightingale or the lark. Romeo leaves. Lady Capulet tells Juliet of the wedding; Juliet refuses. Capulet threatens to throw her out. The Nurse advises marrying Paris; Juliet decides to seek the Friar's help, or die.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior

Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the scene's imagery and foreshadowing), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how William Shakespeare uses imagery in Act III, Scene V to complicate the reader's understanding of parting at dawn and Capulet's rage. writingPrompts.label: College Freshman

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore

Argue how the scene's handling of parting at dawn and Capulet's rage follows or bends those conventions, using the imagery as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Act III, Scene V and its treatment of parting at dawn and Capulet's rage. State your method, show what it reveals in the scene's imagery and foreshadowing, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Act III, Scene V as evidence for a larger claim about parting at dawn and Capulet's rage in Romeo and Juliet. Connect close reading of the scene to the whole play, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Act III, Scene V as a hinge in the play's larger treatment of parting at dawn and Capulet's rage. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Romeo and Juliet.

symbolsAndMotifs.name: light and dark
symbolsAndMotifs.explanation: The lovers describe each other as light in darkness (torches, sun, stars, lightning), yet they can meet only at night, and daylight brings danger. In this scene: “Wilt thou be gone? it is not yet near day: / It was the nightingale, and not the lark, / That pierced the” (Act III, Scene V, Juliet (speech 1)).

symbolsAndMotifs.name: fate and the stars
symbolsAndMotifs.explanation: From "star-cross'd" in the Prologue to Romeo's "I defy you, stars," the lovers feel steered by fortune, while the plot shows human choices and accidents. In this scene: “is not the lark, whose notes do beat / The vaulty heaven so high above our heads: / I have more care to stay” (Act III, Scene V, Romeo (speech 4)).

segments.activity: Independent annotation and a claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph (exemplar given).
segments.script: Annotate the scene for imagery, foreshadowing (three marks with a margin note each), then write one claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph: what does this scene suggest about parting at dawn and Capulet's rage? Then start your writing prompt at your assigned level (HS Sophomore: Analyze how Act III, Scene V develops the idea of parting at dawn and Capulet's rage. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of imagery and foreshadowing shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.) Exemplar: The scene isolates Juliet completely. When the text says “Hang thee, young baggage! disobedient wretch” (Act III, Scene V, Capulet (speech 49)), it shows this directly. After she sees Romeo "As one dead in the bottom of a tomb," her father calls her "young baggage! disobedient wretch," her mother refuses to help and the Nurse tells her to marry Paris.

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the scene to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.
